Conceptual Affinity. Certain bits of code want to be near other bits. They
have a certain conceptual affinity. The stronger that affinity, the less vertical
distance there should be between them.

As we have seen, this affinity might be based on a direct dependence, such
as one function calling another, or a function using a variable. But there are
other possible causes of affinity. Affinity might be caused because a group
of functions perform a similar operation. Consider this snippet of code from
Junit 4.3.1:



   public class Assert {
     static public void assertTrue(String message, boolean condition) {
       if (!condition)
         fail(message);
     }

     static public void assertTrue(boolean condition) {
       assertTrue(null, condition);
     }

     static public void assertFalse(String message, boolean condition) {
       assertTrue(message, !condition);
     }

     static public void assertFalse(boolean condition) {
       assertFalse(null, condition);
     }
   …

These functions have a strong conceptual affinity because they share a
common naming scheme and perform variations of the same basic task. The
fact that they call each other is secondary. Even if they didn’t, they would
still want to be close together.

Vertical Ordering

In general we want function call dependencies to point in the downward
direction. That is, a function that is called should be below a function that
does the calling.2 This creates a nice flow down the source code module
from high level to low level.
2. This is the exact opposite of languages like Pascal, C, and C++ that enforce functions to be
defined, or at least declared, before they are used.

As in newspaper articles, we expect the most important concepts to come
first, and we expect them to be expressed with the least amount of polluting
detail. We expect the low-level details to come last. This allows us to skim
source files, getting the gist from the first few functions, without having to
immerse ourselves in the details. Listing 5-5 is organized this way. Perhaps
even better examples are Listing 15-5 on page 263, and Listing 3-7 on page
50.



Horizontal Formatting

How wide should a line be? To answer that, let’s look at how wide lines are
in typical programs. Again, we examine the seven different projects. Figure
5-2 shows the distribution of line lengths of all seven projects. The
regularity is impressive, especially right around 45 characters. Indeed,
every size from 20 to 60 represents about 1 percent of the total number of
lines. That’s 40 percent! Perhaps another 30 percent are less than 10
characters wide. Remember this is a log scale, so the linear appearance of
the drop-off above 80 characters is really very significant. Programmers
clearly prefer short lines.

Figure 5-2 Java line width distribution

This suggests that we should strive to keep our lines short. The old
Hollerith limit of 80 is a bit arbitrary, and I’m not opposed to lines edging
out to 100 or even 120. But beyond that is probably just careless.

I used to follow the rule that you should never have to scroll to the right.
But monitors are too wide for that nowadays, and younger programmers
can shrink the font so small that they can get 200 characters across the
screen. Don’t do that. I personally set my limit at 120.



Horizontal Openness and Density

We use horizontal white space to associate things that are strongly related
and disassociate things that are more weakly related. Consider the following
function:
   private void measureLine(String line) {
     lineCount++;
     int lineSize = line.length();
     totalChars += lineSize;
     lineWidthHistogram.addLine(lineSize, lineCount);
     recordWidestLine(lineSize);
   }

I surrounded the assignment operators with white space to accentuate them.
Assignment statements have two distinct and major elements: the left side

2. **`withKeepAliveInterval(30)`**  
   - Configures the interval (in seconds) at which the client sends a "ping" message to the server to keep the connection alive.  
   - The purpose is to prevent intermediate network devices (e.g., routers, proxies) from closing idle connections.  
   - Setting it to `30` means the client will send a keep-alive message every 30 seconds.

3. **`setHttpClientBuilderCallback()`**

   - If the server does not send any message within this timeout period, the client triggers reconnection or error handling logic.  
   - This prevents the client from hanging indefinitely if the server stops responding.

5. **`withAutomaticReconnect()`**  
   - Enables automatic reconnection logic.

- `setHttpClientBuilderCallback()` provides a hook to customize the HTTP client settings used by the SignalR connection.  
- `withServerTimeout()` defines how long the client waits without receiving messages from the server before timing out.

The method `setHttpClientBuilderCallback()` serves as a configuration hook within the SignalR client connection setup, enabling fine-grained customization of the underlying HTTP client used for communication with the SignalR server. This method is typically exposed as part of the client SDK to allow developers to tailor the HTTP client's behavior and capabilities to specific application needs or environment constraints.

### Detailed Explanation of `setHttpClientBuilderCallback()`

1. **Purpose and Context**  
   SignalR connections often use HTTP-based transports such as WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE), or Long Polling to establish and maintain real-time communication between client and server. Underneath these transports is an HTTP client responsible for sending requests, handling responses, managing headers, and dealing with network-level concerns.

   The `setHttpClientBuilderCallback()` method provides a callback interface or lambda function that receives a builder or configuration object for this HTTP client. This allows the developer to programmatically modify the HTTP client's properties prior to the final construction of the SignalR `HubConnection`.

2. **Common Customizations Enabled by this Hook**  
   - **Timeout Settings:** Adjust connection timeouts, read/write timeouts, and overall request duration to optimize responsiveness or tolerance to network conditions.  
   - **HTTP Headers:** Add or modify request headers, such as authentication tokens (e.g., Bearer tokens), custom correlation IDs, or content-type headers.  
   - **Proxy Settings:** Configure HTTP proxy usage if the application environment requires routing through proxies for security or monitoring.  
   - **TLS/SSL Configuration:** Customize SSL context, trust managers, or certificate validation policies to meet security requirements or support custom certificates.  
   - **Logging and Diagnostics:** Enable detailed logging of HTTP requests and responses for debugging or audit trails.  
   - **Connection Pooling:** Tune connection pooling parameters for performance in high-concurrency scenarios.  
   - **Compression and Encoding:** Configure request/response compression to reduce bandwidth usage.

3. **Example Usage (Hypothetical)**  
   ```kotlin
   hubConnection = HubConnectionBuilder
       .create(hubUrl)
       .setHttpClientBuilderCallback { httpClientBuilder ->
           httpClientBuilder
               .connectTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
               .readTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
               .addInterceptor { chain ->
                   val newRequest = chain.request().newBuilder()
                       .addHeader("Authorization", "Bearer your_token_here")
                       .build()
                   chain.proceed(newRequest)
               }
       }
       .build()
   ```
   In this example, the callback receives `httpClientBuilder`, an object to configure the HTTP client. It sets connection and read timeouts, and adds an interceptor to include an Authorization header on each request.

4. **Benefits**  
   - **Flexibility:** Developers can adapt the HTTP client's behavior to diverse environments, such as mobile networks, enterprise firewalls, or secured intranets.  
   - **Security:** Supports injecting custom authentication schemes and enforcing stricter TLS policies.  
   - **Performance:** Enables optimization for latency, throughput, and resource consumption according to the application's profile.  
   - **Maintainability:** Centralizes HTTP client configuration in one place, improving code clarity and simplifying updates.

5. **Implementation Considerations**  
   - The exact type of the HTTP client builder and its available methods depend on the specific SignalR client library version and underlying HTTP client implementation (e.g., OkHttp for Kotlin/Java).  
   - Developers should ensure that customizations do not conflict with SignalR's internal transport mechanisms or expected behaviors.  
   - Proper error handling within the callback is recommended to avoid connection failures due to misconfiguration.

---

### Conclusion

`setHttpClientBuilderCallback()` is a powerful extension point within the SignalR client builder pattern that empowers developers to configure the HTTP client at a granular level. It bridges the gap between SignalR’s real-time communication features and the low-level HTTP transport, enabling enhanced security, performance tuning, and environmental adaptability tailored to the application’s requirements.

---

### Causes

1. **Build Cache Corruption or Conflicts**  
   Multiple KSP instances or build processes might be overlapping or stale cache files are causing conflicts.

2. **Concurrent Builds or IDE Sync Issues**  
   Parallel or incremental builds or IDE background syncs can cause the same cache to be registered multiple times.

3. **Misconfiguration in Build Scripts**  
   The KSP plugin or Gradle build script might be configured incorrectly, causing repeated registration.

---

### Recommended Solutions

1. **Clean and Rebuild the Project**  
   Remove stale build artifacts and caches:  
   ```bash
   ./gradlew clean
   ```  
   Then rebuild the project to regenerate caches properly.

2. **Invalidate IDE Caches**  
   In IntelliJ IDEA or Android Studio:  
   - Go to **File > Invalidate Caches / Restart**  
   - Select **Invalidate and Restart**  
   This clears IDE internal caches that may conflict with KSP caches.

3. **Check for Duplicate KSP Plugin Versions**  
   Make sure your `build.gradle` files do not apply multiple versions of KSP or have conflicting configurations.

4. **Disable Parallel Compilation (Temporarily)**  
   Sometimes parallel build tasks cause conflicts. You can disable it in your `gradle.properties`:  
   ```
   org.gradle.parallel=false
   ```

5. **Delete KSP Cache Folder Manually**  
   Delete the folder at:  
   ```
   D:\Deployment\Logistixs_v6\application\build\kspCaches\
   ```  
   to force regeneration on next build.

6. **Update KSP Plugin**  
   If using an older version of KSP, consider upgrading to the latest stable version, as some bugs related to caching and concurrency have been fixed in recent releases.

---

This exception occurs because KSP attempts to register the same cache storage twice. Cleaning caches, invalidating IDE caches, verifying build configuration, and controlling parallelism usually resolve it.

---

### 2. **Set `JAVA_HOME` Environment Variable to 64-bit JDK**

After installation:

- Open **System Properties**:
  - Windows: Right-click **This PC** → **Properties** → **Advanced system settings** → **Environment Variables**
- Under **System variables**, locate or create `JAVA_HOME`
  - Set its value to the path of your 64-bit JDK, e.g.:  
    ```
    C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-<version>
    ```
- Ensure the `Path` variable includes `%JAVA_HOME%\bin` before any other Java paths.

```
Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 1.8.0_xxx-bxx)

```

If it says **64-Bit**, you are running the 64-bit JVM.

After these changes:

```bash
gradlew --stop
gradlew clean
```

- Build your project again:

```bash
gradlew build
```

thoughts.content: It looks like the Java client indeed doesn't support the `withAutomaticReconnect()` feature. After checking the Javadoc for `HubConnectionBuilder`, I found that it only allows for two methods: `build()` and `create(String url)`. The `create` method then leads to `HttpHubConnectionBuilder`. After reviewing the available methods for `HttpHubConnectionBuilder`, none of them include `withAutomaticReconnect`. So, it's clear that this feature isn’t available in the Java client library.

parts:
I have verified against the official Java (and thus Android) SignalR client API. In the `com.microsoft.signalr` library (e.g. version 5.0.10), the `HttpHubConnectionBuilder` class exposes only the following configuration methods:

- `build()`  
- `setHttpClientBuilderCallback(Action1<OkHttpClient.Builder>)`  
- `shouldSkipNegotiate(boolean)`  
- `withAccessTokenProvider(Single<String>)`  
- `withHandshakeResponseTimeout(long)`  
- `withHeader(String, String)` / `withHeaders(Map<String,String>)`  
- `withHubProtocol(HubProtocol)`  
- `withTransport(TransportEnum)`  

There is no `withAutomaticReconnect()` overload listed in this Java API reference citeturn7view0L3-L7. Automatic-reconnect support is currently provided in the .NET and JavaScript clients, but the Android (Java) client does not include a built-in `withAutomaticReconnect()` method. 

To achieve automatic reconnection on Android, you must implement your own reconnect logic (e.g. handling `HubConnection.onClosed` and restarting the connection) or wrap the connection start in a retry mechanism.

## 1. Verify Your SignalR Artifact Coordinates  
Please share the exact Maven/Gradle dependency you have for SignalR, for example:

```gradle
implementation "com.microsoft.signalr:signalr:<version>"
```

Knowing your `<version>` will allow me to confirm exactly which builder methods are available in your environment.

---

## 2. Manual Reconnect Implementation  
Since the Android/Java SignalR client does not include a built-in `withAutomaticReconnect()`, you can implement a simple retry loop around connection failures:

```kotlin
private fun setupSignalRConnection() {
    hubConnection = HubConnectionBuilder
        .create(hubUrl)
        .setHttpClientBuilderCallback { clientBuilder ->
            // your custom HTTP client configuration here
        }
        .withServerTimeout(60_000)          // e.g. 60 s
        .build()

    hubConnection.onClosed { error ->
        // Log the error if any
        Timber.e(error, "SignalR connection closed; scheduling reconnect")

        // Schedule a reconnect attempt after a delay
        GlobalScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            delay(5_000)  // 5 seconds back-off
            try {
                hubConnection.start().blockingAwait()
                Timber.i("SignalR reconnected successfully")
            } catch (ex: Exception) {
                Timber.e(ex, "SignalR reconnect attempt failed")
                // Optionally schedule another retry or escalate
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### How it Works  
1. **`onClosed { error -> … }`**  
   Registers a callback invoked whenever the connection terminates (cleanly or due to error).  
2. **`delay(5_000)`**  
   Implements a simple fixed back-off before retrying. You can increase this or implement exponential back-off.  
3. **`start().blockingAwait()`**  
   Attempts to re-establish the connection synchronously; errors are caught and logged.  

---

## 3. Next Steps  
1. **Provide your current SignalR client version** so I can tailor any further API references.  
2. **Adjust the back-off and retry policy** as needed for your application’s reliability requirements.

parts:
The call to `join()` comes from Java’s `CompletableFuture` API. In the code I provided, `hubConnection.start()` returns a `CompletableFuture<Void>`, so calling `join()` will block the current thread until that future completes (or throws an unchecked exception). It’s essentially equivalent to:

```java
hubConnection.start().get();  // but rethrows checked exceptions as unchecked
```

---

### Why `join()` appeared

- **SignalR Java/Android client**: the `start()` and `stop()` methods return `CompletableFuture<Void>`, not an RxJava `Completable` or `Single`.  
- **Blocking until connected**: to preserve your original synchronous flow (you were using `blockingAwait()` on an Rx type), you need some way to block on the `CompletableFuture`.  
- **Choice of `join()`**:  
  - `join()` blocks the thread until the future completes, then returns the result (or throws a `CompletionException` on failure).  
  - It avoids you having to catch checked `ExecutionException` / `InterruptedException` explicitly.  

---

### If you’d rather keep using `blockingAwait()`

That method is part of RxJava’s bridge (`kotlinx-coroutines-rx2` or similar). If your project already brings in an Rx–Coroutines adapter and you prefer:

```kotlin
hubConnection.start().blockingAwait()
hubConnection.stop().blockingAwait()
```

you can simply replace `.join()` with `.blockingAwait()` again—just ensure you have the Rx2–Coroutines bridge dependency:

```groovy
implementation "org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-rx2:1.x.x"
```

and import:

```kotlin
import kotlinx.coroutines.rx2.await
```

or the appropriate Rx2 extension.

---

### Summary

- **`join()`** was introduced because `HubConnection.start()` returns a `CompletableFuture`.  
- It blocks until the connection is established, much like your previous `blockingAwait()`.  
- If you prefer **RxJava’s** `blockingAwait()`, simply revert to that—provided you include the Rx–Coroutines adapter in your Gradle.

[L1] Consider the calling hierarchy of a large system. Functions at the top call
[L2] functions below them, which call more functions below them, ad infinitum.
[L3] Now let’s say one of the lowest level functions is modified in such a way
[L4] that it must throw an exception. If that exception is checked, then the
[L5] function signature must add a throws clause. But this means that every
[L6] function that calls our modified function must also be modified either to
[L7] catch the new exception or to append the appropriate throws clause to its
[L8] signature. Ad infinitum. The net result is a cascade of changes that work
[L9] their way from the lowest levels of the software to the highest!
[L10] Encapsulation is broken because all functions in the path of a throw must
[L11] know about details of that low-level exception. Given that the purpose of
[L12] 
[L13] 
[L14] 
[L15] exceptions is to allow you to handle errors at a distance, it is a shame that
[L16] checked exceptions break encapsulation in this way.
[L17] 
[L18] Checked exceptions can sometimes be useful if you are writing a critical
[L19] library: You must catch them. But in general application development the
[L20] dependency costs outweigh the benefits.
[L21] 
[L22] 
[L23] 
[L24] Provide Context with Exceptions
[L25] 
[L26] Each exception that you throw should provide enough context to determine
[L27] the source and location of an error. In Java, you can get a stack trace from
[L28] any exception; however, a stack trace can’t tell you the intent of the
[L29] operation that failed.
[L30] 
[L31] Create informative error messages and pass them along with your
[L32] exceptions. Mention the operation that failed and the type of failure. If you
[L33] are logging in your application, pass along enough information to be able to
[L34] log the error in your catch.
[L35] 
[L36] 
[L37] 
[L38] Define Exception Classes in Terms of a Caller’s Needs
[L39] 
[L40] There are many ways to classify errors. We can classify them by their
[L41] source: Did they come from one component or another? Or their type: Are
[L42] they device failures, network failures, or programming errors? However,
[L43] when we define exception classes in an application, our most important
[L44] concern should be how they are caught.
[L45] 
[L46] Let’s look at an example of poor exception classification. Here is a try-catch-
[L47] finally statement for a third-party library call. It covers all of the exceptions
[L48] that the calls can throw:
[L49]    ACMEPort port = new ACMEPort(12);
[L50] 
[L51]    try {
[L52]      port.open();
[L53]    } catch (DeviceResponseException e) {
[L54]      reportPortError(e);
[L55]      logger.log(“Device response exception”, e);
[L56]    } catch (ATM1212UnlockedException e) {
[L57]      reportPortError(e);
[L58]      logger.log(“Unlock exception”, e);
[L59]    } catch (GMXError e) {
[L60]      reportPortError(e);
[L61]      logger.log(“Device response exception”);
[L62]    } finally {
[L63]      …
[L64]    }
[L65] 
[L66] That statement contains a lot of duplication, and we shouldn’t be surprised.
[L67] In most exception handling situations, the work that we do is relatively
[L68] standard regardless of the actual cause. We have to record an error and
[L69] make sure that we can proceed.
[L70] 
[L71] In this case, because we know that the work that we are doing is roughly the
[L72] same regardless of the exception, we can simplify our code considerably by
[L73] wrapping the API that we are calling and making sure that it returns a
[L74] common exception type:
[L75]    LocalPort port = new LocalPort(12);
[L76]    try {
[L77]      port.open();
[L78]    } catch (PortDeviceFailure e) {
[L79]      reportError(e);
[L80]      logger.log(e.getMessage(), e);
[L81]    } finally {
[L82]      …
[L83]    }
[L84] 
[L85] Our LocalPort class is just a simple wrapper that catches and translates
[L86] exceptions thrown by the ACMEPort class:
[L87] 
[L88] 
[L89] 
[L90]    public class LocalPort {
[L91]      private ACMEPort innerPort;
[L92] 
[L93]      public LocalPort(int portNumber) {
[L94]        innerPort = new ACMEPort(portNumber);
[L95]      }

[L21] Dependency Injection
[L22] 
[L23] A powerful mechanism for separating construction from use is Dependency
[L24] Injection (DI), the application of Inversion of Control (IoC) to dependency
[L25] management.3 Inversion of Control moves secondary responsibilities from
[L26] an object to other objects that are dedicated to the purpose, thereby
[L27] supporting the Single Responsibility Principle. In the context of dependency
[L28] management, an object should not take responsibility for instantiating
[L29] dependencies itself. Instead, it should pass this responsibility to another
[L30] “authoritative” mechanism, thereby inverting the control. Because setup is a
[L31] global concern, this authoritative mechanism will usually be either the
[L32] “main” routine or a special-purpose container.
[L33] 3. See, for example, [Fowler].
[L34] 
[L35] JNDI lookups are a “partial” implementation of DI, where an object asks a
[L36] directory server to provide a “service” matching a particular name.
[L37]    MyService myService = (MyService)(jndiContext.lookup(“NameOfMyService”));
[L38] 
[L39] The invoking object doesn’t control what kind of object is actually returned
[L40] (as long it implements the appropriate interface, of course), but the invoking
[L41] 
[L42] 
[L43] 
[L44] object still actively resolves the dependency.
[L45] 
[L46] True Dependency Injection goes one step further. The class takes no direct
[L47] steps to resolve its dependencies; it is completely passive. Instead, it
[L48] provides setter methods or constructor arguments (or both) that are used to
[L49] inject the dependencies. During the construction process, the DI container
[L50] instantiates the required objects (usually on demand) and uses the
[L51] constructor arguments or setter methods provided to wire together the
[L52] dependencies. Which dependent objects are actually used is specified
[L53] through a configuration file or programmatically in a special-purpose
[L54] construction module.
[L55] 
[L56] The Spring Framework provides the best known DI container for Java.4
[L57] You define which objects to wire together in an XML configuration file,
[L58] then you ask for particular objects by name in Java code. We will look at an
[L59] example shortly.
[L60] 4. See [Spring]. There is also a Spring.NET framework.
[L61] 
[L62] But what about the virtues of LAZY-INITIALIZATION? This idiom is still
[L63] sometimes useful with DI. First, most DI containers won’t construct an
[L64] object until needed. Second, many of these containers provide mechanisms
[L65] for invoking factories or for constructing proxies, which could be used for
[L66] LAZY-EVALUATION and similar optimizations.5
[L67] 
[L68] 5. Don’t forget that lazy instantiation/evaluation is just an optimization and
[L69] perhaps premature!
[L70] 
[L71]

[L73] Scaling Up
[L74] 
[L75] Cities grow from towns, which grow from settlements. At first the roads are
[L76] narrow and practically nonexistent, then they are paved, then widened over
[L77] time. Small buildings and empty plots are filled with larger buildings, some
[L78] of which will eventually be replaced with skyscrapers.
[L79] 
[L80] At first there are no services like power, water, sewage, and the Internet
[L81] (gasp!). These services are also added as the population and building
[L82] densities increase.

[L7] One occurrence of LAZY-INITIALIZATION isn’t a serious problem, of course.
[L8] However, there are normally many instances of little setup idioms like this
[L9] in applications. Hence, the global setup strategy (if there is one) is scattered
[L10] across the application, with little modularity and often significant
[L11] duplication.
[L12] 
[L13] If we are diligent about building well-formed and robust systems, we
[L14] should never let little, convenient idioms lead to modularity breakdown.
[L15] The startup process of object construction and wiring is no exception. We
[L16] should modularize this process separately from the normal runtime logic
[L17] and we should make sure that we have a global, consistent strategy for
[L18] resolving our major dependencies.
[L19] 
[L20] Separation of Main
[L21] 
[L22] One way to separate construction from use is simply to move all aspects of
[L23] construction to main, or modules called by main, and to design the rest of the
[L24] system assuming that all objects have been constructed and wired up
[L25] appropriately. (See Figure 11-1.)
[L26] 
[L27] The flow of control is easy to follow. The main function builds the objects
[L28] necessary for the system, then passes them to the application, which simply
[L29] uses them. Notice the direction of the dependency arrows crossing the
[L30] barrier between main and the application. They all go one direction, pointing
[L31] 
[L32] 
[L33] 
[L34] away from main. This means that the application has no knowledge of main
[L35] or of the construction process. It simply expects that everything has been
[L36] built properly.

[L1] The use of accessor functions confuses the issue. If the code had been
[L2] written as follows, then we probably wouldn’t be asking about Demeter
[L3] violations.
[L4]    final String outputDir = ctxt.options.scratchDir.absolutePath;
[L5] 
[L6] This issue would be a lot less confusing if data structures simply had public
[L7] variables and no functions, whereas objects had private variables and public
[L8] functions. However, there are frameworks and standards (e.g., “beans”) that
[L9] demand that even simple data structures have accessors and mutators.
[L10] 
[L11] Hybrids
[L12] 
[L13] This confusion sometimes leads to unfortunate hybrid structures that are
[L14] half object and half data structure. They have functions that do significant
[L15] things, and they also have either public variables or public accessors and
[L16] mutators that, for all intents and purposes, make the private variables
[L17] public, tempting other external functions to use those variables the way a
[L18] procedural program would use a data structure.4
[L19] 
[L20] 4. This is sometimes called Feature Envy from [Refactoring].
[L21] 
[L22] Such hybrids make it hard to add new functions but also make it hard to add
[L23] new data structures. They are the worst of both worlds. Avoid creating
[L24] 
[L25] 
[L26] 
[L27] them. They are indicative of a muddled design whose authors are unsure of
[L28] —or worse, ignorant of—whether they need protection from functions or
[L29] types.
[L30] 
[L31] Hiding Structure
[L32] 
[L33] What if ctxt, options, and scratchDir are objects with real behavior? Then, because
[L34] objects are supposed to hide their internal structure, we should not be able
[L35] to navigate through them. How then would we get the absolute path of the
[L36] scratch directory?
[L37]    ctxt.getAbsolutePathOfScratchDirectoryOption();
[L38] 
[L39] or
[L40]    ctx.getScratchDirectoryOption().getAbsolutePath()
[L41] 
[L42] The first option could lead to an explosion of methods in the ctxt object.
[L43] The second presumes that getScratchDirectoryOption() returns a data structure, not an
[L44] object. Neither option feels good.
[L45] 
[L46] If ctxt is an object, we should be telling it to do something; we should not be
[L47] asking it about its internals. So why did we want the absolute path of the
[L48] scratch directory? What were we going to do with it? Consider this code
[L49] from (many lines farther down in) the same module:
[L50]    String outFile = outputDir + “/” + className.replace('.', '/') + “.class”;
[L51]    FileOutputStream fout = new FileOutputStream(outFile);
[L52]    BufferedOutputStream bos = new BufferedOutputStream(fout);
[L53] 
[L54] The admixture of different levels of detail [G34][G6] is a bit troubling.
[L55] Dots, slashes, file extensions, and File objects should not be so carelessly
[L56] mixed together, and mixed with the enclosing code. Ignoring that, however,
[L57] we see that the intent of getting the absolute path of the scratch directory
[L58] was to create a scratch file of a given name.
[L59] 
[L60] So, what if we told the ctxt object to do this?
[L61]    BufferedOutputStream bos = ctxt.createScratchFileStream(classFileName);
[L62] 
[L63] That seems like a reasonable thing for an object to do! This allows ctxt to
[L64] hide its internals and prevents the current function from having to violate
[L65] the Law of Demeter by navigating through objects it shouldn’t know about.
[L66] 
[L67] 
[L68] 
[L69] Data Transfer Objects
[L70] 
[L71] The quintessential form of a data structure is a class with public variables
[L72] and no functions. This is sometimes called a data transfer object, or DTO.
[L73] DTOs are very useful structures, especially when communicating with
[L74] databases or parsing messages from sockets, and so on. They often become
[L75] the first in a series of translation stages that convert raw data in a database
[L76] into objects in the application code.
[L77] 
[L78] Somewhat more common is the “bean” form shown in Listing 6-7. Beans
[L79] have private variables manipulated by getters and setters. The quasi-
[L80] encapsulation of beans seems to make some OO purists feel better but
[L81] usually provides no other benefit.

[L1] Fortunately, Java has Collections.emptyList(), and it returns a predefined
[L2] immutable list that we can use for this purpose:
[L3]    public List<Employee> getEmployees() {
[L4]      if( .. there are no employees .. )
[L5]        return Collections.emptyList();
[L6]    }
[L7] 
[L8] If you code this way, you will minimize the chance of NullPointerExceptions and
[L9] your code will be cleaner.
[L10] 
[L11] 
[L12] 
[L13] Don’t Pass Null
[L14] 
[L15] Returning null from methods is bad, but passing null into methods is worse.
[L16] Unless you are working with an API which expects you to pass null, you
[L17] should avoid passing null in your code whenever possible.
[L18] 
[L19] Let’s look at an example to see why. Here is a simple method which
[L20] calculates a metric for two points:
[L21]    public class MetricsCalculator
[L22]    {
[L23]      public double xProjection(Point p1, Point p2) {
[L24]        return (p2.x – p1.x) * 1.5;
[L25]      }
[L26]      …
[L27]    }
[L28] 
[L29] What happens when someone passes null as an argument?
[L30]    calculator.xProjection(null, new Point(12, 13));
[L31] 
[L32] We’ll get a NullPointerException, of course.
[L33] 
[L34] How can we fix it? We could create a new exception type and throw it:
[L35]    public class MetricsCalculator
[L36]    {
[L37]     public double xProjection(Point p1, Point p2) {
[L38]       if (p1 == null || p2 == null) {
[L39]          throw InvalidArgumentException(
[L40]            “Invalid argument for MetricsCalculator.xProjection”);
[L41]       }
[L42]       return (p2.x – p1.x) * 1.5;
[L43]     }
[L44]    }
[L45] 
[L46] Is this better? It might be a little better than a null pointer exception, but
[L47] remember, we have to define a handler for InvalidArgumentException. What should
[L48] the handler do? Is there any good course of action?
[L49] 
[L50] There is another alternative. We could use a set of assertions:
[L51]    public class MetricsCalculator
[L52]    {
[L53]      public double xProjection(Point p1, Point p2) {
[L54]        assert p1 != null : “p1 should not be null”;
[L55]        assert p2 != null : “p2 should not be null”;
[L56]        return (p2.x – p1.x) * 1.5;
[L57]      }
[L58]    }
[L59] 
[L60] It’s good documentation, but it doesn’t solve the problem. If someone
[L61] passes null, we’ll still have a runtime error.
[L62] 
[L63] 
[L64] 
[L65] In most programming languages there is no good way to deal with a null that
[L66] is passed by a caller accidentally. Because this is the case, the rational
[L67] approach is to forbid passing null by default. When you do, you can code
[L68] with the knowledge that a null in an argument list is an indication of a
[L69] problem, and end up with far fewer careless mistakes.
[L70] 
[L71] 
[L72] 
[L73] Conclusion
[L74] 
[L75] Clean code is readable, but it must also be robust. These are not conflicting
[L76] goals. We can write robust clean code if we see error handling as a separate
[L77] concern, something that is viewable independently of our main logic. To the
[L78] degree that we are able to do that, we can reason about it independently, and
[L79] we can make great strides in the maintainability of our code.
[L80] 
[L81]

[L86] Robert C. Martin, Prentice Hall, 2002.

[L1] Finally, you had to write one or more XML deployment descriptors that
[L2] specify the object-relational mapping details to a persistence store, the
[L3] desired transactional behavior, security constraints, and so on.
[L4] 
[L5] The business logic is tightly coupled to the EJB2 application “container.”
[L6] You must subclass container types and you must provide many lifecycle
[L7] methods that are required by the container.
[L8] 
[L9] Because of this coupling to the heavyweight container, isolated unit testing
[L10] is difficult. It is necessary to mock out the container, which is hard, or waste
[L11] a lot of time deploying EJBs and tests to a real server. Reuse outside of the
[L12] EJB2 architecture is effectively impossible, due to the tight coupling.
[L13] 
[L14] Finally, even object-oriented programming is undermined. One bean cannot
[L15] inherit from another bean. Notice the logic for adding a new account. It is
[L16] common in EJB2 beans to define “data transfer objects” (DTOs) that are
[L17] essentially “structs” with no behavior. This usually leads to redundant types
[L18] holding essentially the same data, and it requires boilerplate code to copy
[L19] data from one object to another.
[L20] 
[L21] Cross-Cutting Concerns
[L22] 
[L23] The EJB2 architecture comes close to true separation of concerns in some
[L24] areas. For example, the desired transactional, security, and some of the
[L25] persistence behaviors are declared in the deployment descriptors,
[L26] independently of the source code.
[L27] 
[L28] Note that concerns like persistence tend to cut across the natural object
[L29] boundaries of a domain. You want to persist all your objects using generally
[L30] 
[L31] 
[L32] 
[L33] the same strategy, for example, using a particular DBMS6 versus flat files,
[L34] following certain naming conventions for tables and columns, using
[L35] consistent transactional semantics, and so on.
[L36] 6. Database management system.
[L37] 
[L38] In principle, you can reason about your persistence strategy in a modular,
[L39] encapsulated way. Yet, in practice, you have to spread essentially the same
[L40] code that implements the persistence strategy across many objects. We use
[L41] the term cross-cutting concerns for concerns like these. Again, the
[L42] persistence framework might be modular and our domain logic, in isolation,
[L43] might be modular. The problem is the fine-grained intersection of these
[L44] domains.
[L45] 
[L46] In fact, the way the EJB architecture handled persistence, security, and
[L47] transactions, “anticipated” aspect-oriented programming (AOP),7 which is
[L48] a general-purpose approach to restoring modularity for cross-cutting
[L49] concerns.
[L50] 7. See [AOSD] for general information on aspects and [AspectJ]] and [Colyer] for AspectJ-specific
[L51] information.
[L52] 
[L53] In AOP, modular constructs called aspects specify which points in the
[L54] system should have their behavior modified in some consistent way to
[L55] support a particular concern. This specification is done using a succinct
[L56] declarative or programmatic mechanism.
[L57] 
[L58] Using persistence as an example, you would declare which objects and
[L59] attributes (or patterns thereof) should be persisted and then delegate the
[L60] persistence tasks to your persistence framework. The behavior
[L61] modifications are made noninvasively8 to the target code by the AOP
[L62] framework. Let us look at three aspects or aspect-like mechanisms in Java.

[L1] This clarifies the issue, but only at the expense of checking the declaration
[L2] of the function. Anything that forces you to check the function signature is
[L3] equivalent to a double-take. It’s a cognitive break and should be avoided.
[L4] 
[L5] In the days before object oriented programming it was sometimes necessary
[L6] to have output arguments. However, much of the need for output arguments
[L7] disappears in OO languages because this is intended to act as an output
[L8] argument. In other words, it would be better for appendFooter to be invoked as
[L9]    report.appendFooter();
[L10] 
[L11] In general output arguments should be avoided. If your function must
[L12] change the state of something, have it change the state of its owning object.
[L13] 
[L14] 
[L15] 
[L16] Command Query Separation
[L17] 
[L18] Functions should either do something or answer something, but not both.
[L19] Either your function should change the state of an object, or it should return
[L20] some information about that object. Doing both often leads to confusion.
[L21] Consider, for example, the following function:
[L22]    public boolean set(String attribute, String value);
[L23] 
[L24] This function sets the value of a named attribute and returns true if it is
[L25] successful and false if no such attribute exists. This leads to odd statements
[L26] like this:
[L27]    if (set(”username”, ”unclebob”))…
[L28] 
[L29] Imagine this from the point of view of the reader. What does it mean? Is it
[L30] asking whether the “username” attribute was previously set to “unclebob”? Or is it
[L31] asking whether the “username” attribute was successfully set to “unclebob”? It’s
[L32] hard to infer the meaning from the call because it’s not clear whether the
[L33] word “set” is a verb or an adjective.
[L34] 
[L35] The author intended set to be a verb, but in the context of the if statement it
[L36] feels like an adjective. So the statement reads as “If the username attribute was
[L37] previously set to unclebob” and not “set the username attribute to unclebob and if that
[L38] worked then.…” We could try to resolve this by renaming the set function to
[L39] setAndCheckIfExists, but that doesn’t much help the readability of the if statement.
[L40] The real solution is to separate the command from the query so that the
[L41] ambiguity cannot occur.
[L42]    if (attributeExists(”username”)) {
[L43]      setAttribute(”username”, ”unclebob”);
[L44]      …
[L45]    }
[L46] 
[L47] 
[L48] 
[L49] Prefer Exceptions to Returning Error Codes
[L50] 
[L51] Returning error codes from command functions is a subtle violation of
[L52] command query separation. It promotes commands being used as
[L53] expressions in the predicates of if statements.
[L54]    if (deletePage(page) == E_OK)
[L55] 
[L56] This does not suffer from verb/adjective confusion but does lead to deeply
[L57] nested structures. When you return an error code, you create the problem
[L58] that the caller must deal with the error immediately.
[L59]    if (deletePage(page) == E_OK) {
[L60]      if (registry.deleteReference(page.name) == E_OK) {
[L61]        if (configKeys.deleteKey(page.name.makeKey()) == E_OK){
[L62]          logger.log("page deleted");
[L63]        } else {
[L64]          logger.log("configKey not deleted");
[L65]        }
[L66]      } else {
[L67]        logger.log("deleteReference from registry failed");
[L68]      }
[L69]    } else {
[L70]      logger.log("delete failed");
[L71]      return E_ERROR;
[L72]    }
[L73] 
[L74] On the other hand, if you use exceptions instead of returned error codes,
[L75] then the error processing code can be separated from the happy path code
[L76] and can be simplified:
[L77]    try {
[L78]      deletePage(page);
[L79]      registry.deleteReference(page.name);
[L80]      configKeys.deleteKey(page.name.makeKey());
[L81]    }
[L82]    catch (Exception e) {
[L83]      logger.log(e.getMessage());
[L84]    }

[L849] Foreword
[L850] 
[L851] One of our favorite candies here in Denmark is Ga-Jol, whose strong
[L852] licorice vapors are a perfect complement to our damp and often chilly
[L853] weather. Part of the charm of Ga-Jol to us Danes is the wise or witty
[L854] sayings printed on the flap of every box top. I bought a two-pack of the
[L855] delicacy this morning and found that it bore this old Danish saw:
[L856] 
[L857] Ærlighed i små ting er ikke nogen lille ting.
[L858] 
[L859] “Honesty in small things is not a small thing.” It was a good omen
[L860] consistent with what I already wanted to say here. Small things matter. This
[L861] is a book about humble concerns whose value is nonetheless far from small.
[L862] 
[L863] God is in the details, said the architect Ludwig mies van der Rohe. This
[L864] quote recalls contemporary arguments about the role of architecture in
[L865] software development, and particularly in the Agile world. Bob and I
[L866] occasionally find ourselves passionately engaged in this dialogue. And yes,
[L867] mies van der Rohe was attentive to utility and to the timeless forms of
[L868] building that underlie great architecture. On the other hand, he also
[L869] personally selected every doorknob for every house he designed. Why?
[L870] Because small things matter.
[L871] 
[L872] In our ongoing “debate” on TDD, Bob and I have discovered that we agree
[L873] that software architecture has an important place in development, though
[L874] we likely have different visions of exactly what that means. Such quibbles
[L875] are relatively unimportant, however, because we can accept for granted that
[L876] responsible professionals give some time to thinking and planning at the
[L877] outset of a project. The late-1990s notions of design driven only by the tests
[L878] and the code are long gone. Yet attentiveness to detail is an even more
[L879] critical foundation of professionalism than is any grand vision. First, it is
[L880] through practice in the small that professionals gain proficiency and trust
[L881] for practice in the large. Second, the smallest bit of sloppy construction, of
[L882] the door that does not close tightly or the slightly crooked tile on the floor,
[L883] or even the messy desk, completely dispels the charm of the larger whole.
[L884] That is what clean code is about.
[L885] 
[L886] 
[L887] 
[L888] Still, architecture is just one metaphor for software development, and in
[L889] particular for that part of software that delivers the initial product in the
[L890] same sense that an architect delivers a pristine building. In these days of
[L891] Scrum and Agile, the focus is on quickly bringing product to market. We
[L892] want the factory running at top speed to produce software. These are human
[L893] factories: thinking, feeling coders who are working from a product backlog
[L894] or user story to create product. The manufacturing metaphor looms ever
[L895] strong in such thinking. The production aspects of Japanese auto
[L896] manufacturing, of an assembly-line world, inspire much of Scrum.
[L897] 
[L898] Yet even in the auto industry, the bulk of the work lies not in manufacturing
[L899] but in maintenance—or its avoidance. In software, 80% or more of what we
[L900] do is quaintly called “maintenance”: the act of repair. Rather than
[L901] embracing the typical Western focus on producing good software, we
[L902] should be thinking more like home repairmen in the building industry, or
[L903] auto mechanics in the automotive field. What does Japanese management
[L904] have to say about that?
[L905] 
[L906] In about 1951, a quality approach called Total Productive Maintenance
[L907] (TPM) came on the Japanese scene. Its focus is on maintenance rather than
[L908] on production. One of the major pillars of TPM is the set of so-called 5S
[L909] principles. 5S is a set of disciplines—and here I use the term “discipline”
[L910] instructively. These 5S principles are in fact at the foundations of Lean—
[L911] another buzzword on the Western scene, and an increasingly prominent
[L912] buzzword in software circles. These principles are not an option. As Uncle
[L913] Bob relates in his front matter, good software practice requires such
[L914] discipline: focus, presence of mind, and thinking. It is not always just about
[L915] doing, about pushing the factory equipment to produce at the optimal
[L916] velocity. The 5S philosophy comprises these concepts:
[L917] 
[L918] • Seiri, or organization (think “sort” in English). Knowing where things
[L919] are—using approaches such as suitable naming—is crucial. You think
[L920] naming identifiers isn’t important? Read on in the following chapters.
[L921] 
[L922] • Seiton, or tidiness (think “systematize” in English). There is an old
[L923] American saying: A place for everything, and everything in its place.
[L924] A piece of code should be where you expect to find it—and, if not, you
[L925] should re-factor to get it there.
[L926] 
[L927] 
[L928] 
[L929] • Seiso, or cleaning (think “shine” in English): Keep the workplace free
[L930] of hanging wires, grease, scraps, and waste. What do the authors here
[L931] say about littering your code with comments and commented-out code
[L932] lines that capture history or wishes for the future? Get rid of them.
[L933] 
[L934] • Seiketsu, or standardization: The group agrees about how to keep the
[L935] workplace clean. Do you think this book says anything about having a
[L936] consistent coding style and set of practices within the group? Where do
[L937] those standards come from? Read on.
[L938] 
[L939] • Shutsuke, or discipline (self-discipline). This means having the
[L940] discipline to follow the practices and to frequently reflect on one’s
[L941] work and be willing to change.
[L942] 
[L943] If you take up the challenge—yes, the challenge—of reading and applying
[L944] this book, you’ll come to understand and appreciate the last point. Here, we
[L945] are finally driving to the roots of responsible professionalism in a
[L946] profession that should be concerned with the life cycle of a product. As we
[L947] maintain automobiles and other machines under TPM, breakdown
[L948] maintenance—waiting for bugs to surface—is the exception. Instead, we go
[L949] up a level: inspect the machines every day and fix wearing parts before they
[L950] break, or do the equivalent of the proverbial 10,000-mile oil change to
[L951] forestall wear and tear. In code, refactor mercilessly. You can improve yet
[L952] one level further, as the TPM movement innovated over 50 years ago: build
[L953] machines that are more maintainable in the first place. Making your code
[L954] readable is as important as making it executable. The ultimate practice,
[L955] introduced in TPM circles around 1960, is to focus on introducing entire
[L956] new machines or replacing old ones. As Fred Brooks admonishes us, we
[L957] should probably re-do major software chunks from scratch every seven
[L958] years or so to sweep away creeping cruft. Perhaps we should update
[L959] Brooks’ time constant to an order of weeks, days or hours instead of years.
[L960] That’s where detail lies.
[L961] 
[L962] There is great power in detail, yet there is something humble and profound
[L963] about this approach to life, as we might stereotypically expect from any
[L964] approach that claims Japanese roots. But this is not only an Eastern outlook
[L965] on life; English and American folk wisdom are full of such admonishments.
[L966] The Seiton quote from above flowed from the pen of an Ohio minister who
[L967] literally viewed neatness “as a remedy for every degree of evil.” How about
[L968] 
[L969] 
[L970] 
[L971] Seiso? Cleanliness is next to godliness. As beautiful as a house is, a messy
[L972] desk robs it of its splendor. How about Shutsuke in these small matters? He
[L973] who is faithful in little is faithful in much. How about being eager to re-
[L974] factor at the responsible time, strengthening one’s position for subsequent
[L975] “big” decisions, rather than putting it off? A stitch in time saves nine. The
[L976] early bird catches the worm. Don’t put off until tomorrow what you can do
[L977] today. (Such was the original sense of the phrase “the last responsible
[L978] moment” in Lean until it fell into the hands of software consultants.) How
[L979] about calibrating the place of small, individual efforts in a grand whole?
[L980] Mighty oaks from little acorns grow. Or how about integrating simple
[L981] preventive work into everyday life? An ounce of prevention is worth a
[L982] pound of cure. An apple a day keeps the doctor away. Clean code honors
[L983] the deep roots of wisdom beneath our broader culture, or our culture as it
[L984] once was, or should be, and can be with attentiveness to detail.
[L985] 
[L986] Even in the grand architectural literature we find saws that hark back to
[L987] these supposed details. Think of mies van der Rohe’s doorknobs. That’s
[L988] seiri. That’s being attentive to every variable name. You should name a
[L989] variable using the same care with which you name a first-born child.
[L990] 
[L991] As every homeowner knows, such care and ongoing refinement never come
[L992] to an end. The architect Christopher Alexander—father of patterns and
[L993] pattern languages—views every act of design itself as a small, local act of
[L994] repair. And he views the craftsmanship of fine structure to be the sole
[L995] purview of the architect; the larger forms can be left to patterns and their
[L996] application by the inhabitants. Design is ever ongoing not only as we add a
[L997] new room to a house, but as we are attentive to repainting, replacing worn
[L998] carpets, or upgrading the kitchen sink. Most arts echo analogous sentiments.
[L999] In our search for others who ascribe God’s home as being in the details, we
[L1000] find ourselves in the good company of the 19th century French author
[L1001] Gustav Flaubert. The French poet Paul Valery advises us that a poem is
[L1002] never done and bears continual rework, and to stop working on it is
[L1003] abandonment. Such preoccupation with detail is common to all endeavors
[L1004] of excellence. So maybe there is little new here, but in reading this book
[L1005] you will be challenged to take up good disciplines that you long ago
[L1006] surrendered to apathy or a desire for spontaneity and just “responding to
[L1007] change.”
[L1008] 
[L1009] 
[L1010] 
[L1011] Unfortunately, we usually don’t view such concerns as key cornerstones of
[L1012] the art of programming. We abandon our code early, not because it is done,
[L1013] but because our value system focuses more on outward appearance than on
[L1014] the substance of what we deliver. This inattentiveness costs us in the end: A
[L1015] bad penny always shows up. Research, neither in industry nor in academia,
[L1016] humbles itself to the lowly station of keeping code clean. Back in my days
[L1017] working in the Bell Labs Software Production Research organization
[L1018] (Production, indeed!) we had some back-of-the-envelope findings that
[L1019] suggested that consistent indentation style was one of the most statistically
[L1020] significant indicators of low bug density. We want it to be that architecture
[L1021] or programming language or some other high notion should be the cause of
[L1022] quality; as people whose supposed professionalism owes to the mastery of
[L1023] tools and lofty design methods, we feel insulted by the value that those
[L1024] factory-floor machines, the coders, add through the simple consistent
[L1025] application of an indentation style. To quote my own book of 17 years ago,
[L1026] such style distinguishes excellence from mere competence. The Japanese
[L1027] worldview understands the crucial value of the everyday worker and, more
[L1028] so, of the systems of development that owe to the simple, everyday actions
[L1029] of those workers. Quality is the result of a million selfless acts of care—not
[L1030] just of any great method that descends from the heavens. That these acts are
[L1031] simple doesn’t mean that they are simplistic, and it hardly means that they
[L1032] are easy. They are nonetheless the fabric of greatness and, more so, of
[L1033] beauty, in any human endeavor. To ignore them is not yet to be fully human.
[L1034] 
[L1035] Of course, I am still an advocate of thinking at broader scope, and
[L1036] particularly of the value of architectural approaches rooted in deep domain
[L1037] knowledge and software usability. The book isn’t about that—or, at least, it
[L1038] isn’t obviously about that. This book has a subtler message whose
[L1039] profoundness should not be underappreciated. It fits with the current saw of
[L1040] the really code-based people like Peter Sommerlad, Kevlin Henney and
[L1041] Giovanni Asproni. “The code is the design” and “Simple code” are their
[L1042] mantras. While we must take care to remember that the interface is the
[L1043] program, and that its structures have much to say about our program
[L1044] structure, it is crucial to continuously adopt the humble stance that the
[L1045] design lives in the code. And while rework in the manufacturing metaphor
[L1046] leads to cost, rework in design leads to value. We should view our code as
[L1047] the beautiful articulation of noble efforts of design—design as a process,
[L1048] not a static endpoint. It’s in the code that the architectural metrics of
[L1049] 
[L1050] 
[L1051] 
[L1052] coupling and cohesion play out. If you listen to Larry Constantine describe
[L1053] coupling and cohesion, he speaks in terms of code—not lofty abstract
[L1054] concepts that one might find in UML. Richard Gabriel advises us in his
[L1055] essay, “Abstraction Descant” that abstraction is evil. Code is anti-evil, and
[L1056] clean code is perhaps divine.
[L1057] 
[L1058] Going back to my little box of Ga-Jol, I think it’s important to note that the
[L1059] Danish wisdom advises us not just to pay attention to small things, but also
[L1060] to be honest in small things. This means being honest to the code, honest to
[L1061] our colleagues about the state of our code and, most of all, being honest
[L1062] with ourselves about our code. Did we Do our Best to “leave the
[L1063] campground cleaner than we found it”? Did we re-factor our code before
[L1064] checking in? These are not peripheral concerns but concerns that lie
[L1065] squarely in the center of Agile values. It is a recommended practice in
[L1066] Scrum that re-factoring be part of the concept of “Done.” Neither
[L1067] architecture nor clean code insist on perfection, only on honesty and doing
[L1068] the best we can. To err is human; to forgive, divine. In Scrum, we make
[L1069] everything visible. We air our dirty laundry. We are honest about the state of
[L1070] our code because code is never perfect. We become more fully human,
[L1071] more worthy of the divine, and closer to that greatness in the details.
[L1072] 
[L1073] In our profession, we desperately need all the help we can get. If a clean
[L1074] shop floor reduces accidents, and well-organized shop tools increase
[L1075] productivity, then I’m all for them. As for this book, it is the best pragmatic
[L1076] application of Lean principles to software I have ever seen in print. I
[L1077] expected no less from this practical little group of thinking individuals that
[L1078] has been striving together for years not only to become better, but also to
[L1079] gift their knowledge to the industry in works such as you now find in your
[L1080] hands. It leaves the world a little better than I found it before Uncle Bob
[L1081] sent me the manuscript.
[L1082] 
[L1083] Having completed this exercise in lofty insights, I am off to clean my desk.

[L1090] Introduction
[L1091] 
[L1092] Which door represents your code? Which door represents your team or your
[L1093] company? Why are we in that room? Is this just a normal code review or
[L1094] have we found a stream of horrible problems shortly after going live? Are
[L1095] we debugging in a panic, poring over code that we thought worked? Are
[L1096] customers leaving in droves and managers breathing down our necks? How
[L1097] can we make sure we wind up behind the right door when the going gets
[L1098] tough? The answer is: craftsmanship.
[L1099] 
[L1100] There are two parts to learning craftsmanship: knowledge and work. You
[L1101] must gain the knowledge of principles, patterns, practices, and heuristics
[L1102] 
[L1103] 
[L1104] 
[L1105] that a craftsman knows, and you must also grind that knowledge into your
[L1106] fingers, eyes, and gut by working hard and practicing.
[L1107] 
[L1108] I can teach you the physics of riding a bicycle. Indeed, the classical
[L1109] mathematics is relatively straightforward. Gravity, friction, angular
[L1110] momentum, center of mass, and so forth, can be demonstrated with less
[L1111] than a page full of equations. Given those formulae I could prove to you
[L1112] that bicycle riding is practical and give you all the knowledge you needed to
[L1113] make it work. And you’d still fall down the first time you climbed on that
[L1114] bike.
[L1115] 
[L1116] Coding is no different. We could write down all the “feel good” principles
[L1117] of clean code and then trust you to do the work (in other words, let you fall
[L1118] down when you get on the bike), but then what kind of teachers would that
[L1119] make us, and what kind of student would that make you?
[L1120] 
[L1121] No. That’s not the way this book is going to work.
[L1122] 
[L1123] Learning to write clean code is hard work. It requires more than just the
[L1124] knowledge of principles and patterns. You must sweat over it. You must
[L1125] practice it yourself, and watch yourself fail. You must watch others practice
[L1126] it and fail. You must see them stumble and retrace their steps. You must see
[L1127] them agonize over decisions and see the price they pay for making those
[L1128] decisions the wrong way.
[L1129] 
[L1130] Be prepared to work hard while reading this book. This is not a “feel good”
[L1131] book that you can read on an airplane and finish before you land. This book
[L1132] will make you work, and work hard. What kind of work will you be doing?
[L1133] You’ll be reading code—lots of code. And you will be challenged to think
[L1134] about what’s right about that code and what’s wrong with it. You’ll be asked
[L1135] to follow along as we take modules apart and put them back together again.
[L1136] This will take time and effort; but we think it will be worth it.
[L1137] 
[L1138] We have divided this book into three parts. The first several chapters
[L1139] describe the principles, patterns, and practices of writing clean code. There
[L1140] is quite a bit of code in these chapters, and they will be challenging to read.
[L1141] They’ll prepare you for the second section to come. If you put the book
[L1142] down after reading the first section, good luck to you!
[L1143] 
[L1144] The second part of the book is the harder work. It consists of several case
[L1145] studies of ever-increasing complexity. Each case study is an exercise in
[L1146] 
[L1147] 
[L1148] 
[L1149] cleaning up some code—of transforming code that has some problems into
[L1150] code that has fewer problems. The detail in this section is intense. You will
[L1151] have to flip back and forth between the narrative and the code listings. You
[L1152] will have to analyze and understand the code we are working with and walk
[L1153] through our reasoning for making each change we make. Set aside some
[L1154] time because this should take you days.
[L1155] 
[L1156] The third part of this book is the payoff. It is a single chapter containing a
[L1157] list of heuristics and smells gathered while creating the case studies. As we
[L1158] walked through and cleaned up the code in the case studies, we documented
[L1159] every reason for our actions as a heuristic or smell. We tried to understand
[L1160] our own reactions to the code we were reading and changing, and worked
[L1161] hard to capture why we felt what we felt and did what we did. The result is
[L1162] a knowledge base that desribes the way we think when we write, read, and
[L1163] clean code.
[L1164] 
[L1165] This knowledge base is of limited value if you don’t do the work of
[L1166] carefully reading through the case studies in the second part of this book. In
[L1167] those case studies we have carefully annotated each change we made with
[L1168] forward references to the heuristics. These forward references appear in
[L1169] square brackets like this: [H22]. This lets you see the context in which those
[L1170] heuristics were applied and written! It is not the heuristics themselves that
[L1171] are so valuable, it is the relationship between those heuristics and the
[L1172] discrete decisions we made while cleaning up the code in the case studies.
[L1173] 
[L1174] To further help you with those relationships, we have placed a cross-
[L1175] reference at the end of the book that shows the page number for every
[L1176] forward reference. You can use it to look up each place where a certain
[L1177] heuristic was applied.
[L1178] 
[L1179] If you read the first and third sections and skip over the case studies, then
[L1180] you will have read yet another “feel good” book about writing good

[L1182] following every tiny step, every minute decision—if you put yourself in our
[L1183] place, and force yourself to think along the same paths that we thought, then
[L1184] you will gain a much richer understanding of those principles, patterns,
[L1185] practices, and heuristics. They won’t be “feel good” knowledge any more.
[L1186] They’ll have been ground into your gut, fingers, and heart. They’ll have
[L1187]

[L1287] Clean Code
[L1288] 
[L1289] You are reading this book for two reasons. First, you are a programmer.
[L1290] Second, you want to be a better programmer. Good. We need better
[L1291] programmers.
[L1292] 
[L1293] This is a book about good programming. It is filled with code. We are going
[L1294] to look at code from every different direction. We’ll look down at it from
[L1295] the top, up at it from the bottom, and through it from the inside out. By the
[L1296] time we are done, we’re going to know a lot about code. What’s more, we’ll
[L1297] be able to tell the difference between good code and bad code. We’ll know
[L1298] how to write good code. And we’ll know how to transform bad code into
[L1299] good code.
[L1300] 
[L1301] 
[L1302] 
[L1303] There Will Be Code
[L1304] 
[L1305] One might argue that a book about code is somehow behind the times—that
[L1306] code is no longer the issue; that we should be concerned about models and
[L1307] requirements instead. Indeed some have suggested that we are close to the
[L1308] end of code. That soon all code will be generated instead of written. That
[L1309] programmers simply won’t be needed because business people will
[L1310] generate programs from specifications.
[L1311] 
[L1312] Nonsense! We will never be rid of code, because code represents the details
[L1313] of the requirements. At some level those details cannot be ignored or
[L1314] abstracted; they have to be specified. And specifying requirements in such
[L1315] detail that a machine can execute them is programming. Such a
[L1316] specification is code.
[L1317] 
[L1318] I expect that the level of abstraction of our languages will continue to
[L1319] increase. I also expect that the number of domain-specific languages will
[L1320] continue to grow. This will be a good thing. But it will not eliminate code.
[L1321] Indeed, all the specifications written in these higher level and domain-
[L1322] specific language will be code! It will still need to be rigorous, accurate,
[L1323] and so formal and detailed that a machine can understand and execute it.
[L1324] 
[L1325] The folks who think that code will one day disappear are like
[L1326] mathematicians who hope one day to discover a mathematics that does not
[L1327] have to be formal. They are hoping that one day we will discover a way to
[L1328] create machines that can do what we want rather than what we say. These
[L1329] machines will have to be able to understand us so well that they can
[L1330] translate vaguely specified needs into perfectly executing programs that
[L1331] precisely meet those needs.
[L1332] 
[L1333] This will never happen. Not even humans, with all their intuition and
[L1334] creativity, have been able to create successful systems from the vague

[L1350] Bad Code
[L1351] 
[L1352] I was recently reading the preface to Kent Beck’s book Implementation
[L1353] Patterns.1 He says, “… this book is based on a rather fragile premise: that
[L1354] good code matters….” A fragile premise? I disagree! I think that premise is
[L1355] one of the most robust, supported, and overloaded of all the premises in our
[L1356] craft (and I think Kent knows it). We know good code matters because
[L1357] we’ve had to deal for so long with its lack.
[L1358] 1. [Beck07].
[L1359] 
[L1360] I know of one company that, in the late 80s, wrote a killer app. It was very
[L1361] popular, and lots of professionals bought and used it. But then the release
[L1362] cycles began to stretch. Bugs were not repaired from one release to the next.
[L1363] Load times grew and crashes increased. I remember the day I shut the
[L1364] product down in frustration and never used it again. The company went out
[L1365] of business a short time after that.
[L1366] 
[L1367] 
[L1368] 
[L1369] Two decades later I met one of the early employees of that company and
[L1370] asked him what had happened. The answer confirmed my fears. They had
[L1371] rushed the product to market and had made a huge mess in the code. As
[L1372] they added more and more features, the code got worse and worse until they
[L1373] simply could not manage it any longer. It was the bad code that brought the
[L1374] company down.
[L1375] 
[L1376] Have you ever been significantly impeded by bad code? If you are a
[L1377] programmer of any experience then you’ve felt this impediment many
[L1378] times. Indeed, we have a name for it. We call it wading. We wade through
[L1379] bad code. We slog through a morass of tangled brambles and hidden
[L1380] pitfalls. We struggle to find our way, hoping for some hint, some clue, of
[L1381] what is going on; but all we see is more and more senseless code.
[L1382] 
[L1383] Of course you have been impeded by bad code. So then—why did you
[L1384] write it?
[L1385] 
[L1386] Were you trying to go fast? Were you in a rush? Probably so. Perhaps you
[L1387] felt that you didn’t have time to do a good job; that your boss would be
[L1388] angry with you if you took the time to clean up your code. Perhaps you
[L1389] were just tired of working on this program and wanted it to be over. Or
[L1390] maybe you looked at the backlog of other stuff that you had promised to get
[L1391] done and realized that you needed to slam this module together so you
[L1392] could move on to the next. We’ve all done it.
[L1393] 
[L1394] We’ve all looked at the mess we’ve just made and then have chosen to leave
[L1395] it for another day. We’ve all felt the relief of seeing our messy program
[L1396] work and deciding that a working mess is better than nothing. We’ve all
[L1397] said we’d go back and clean it up later. Of course, in those days we didn’t
[L1398] know LeBlanc’s law: Later equals never.
[L1399]

[L1402] The Total Cost of Owning a Mess
[L1403] 
[L1404] If you have been a programmer for more than two or three years, you have
[L1405] probably been significantly slowed down by someone else’s messy code. If
[L1406] you have been a programmer for longer than two or three years, you have
[L1407] probably been slowed down by messy code. The degree of the slowdown
[L1408] can be significant. Over the span of a year or two, teams that were moving
[L1409] very fast at the beginning of a project can find themselves moving at a
[L1410] snail’s pace. Every change they make to the code breaks two or three other
[L1411] parts of the code. No change is trivial. Every addition or modification to the
[L1412] system requires that the tangles, twists, and knots be “understood” so that
[L1413] more tangles, twists, and knots can be added. Over time the mess becomes
[L1414] so big and so deep and so tall, they can not clean it up. There is no way at
[L1415] all.
[L1416] 
[L1417] As the mess builds, the productivity of the team continues to decrease,
[L1418] asymptotically approaching zero. As productivity decreases, management
[L1419] does the only thing they can; they add more staff to the project in hopes of
[L1420] increasing productivity. But that new staff is not versed in the design of the
[L1421] system. They don’t know the difference between a change that matches the
[L1422] design intent and a change that thwarts the design intent. Furthermore, they,
[L1423] and everyone else on the team, are under horrific pressure to increase
[L1424] productivity. So they all make more and more messes, driving the
[L1425] productivity ever further toward zero. (See Figure 1-1.)

[L1429] The Grand Redesign in the Sky
[L1430] 
[L1431] 
[L1432] 
[L1433] Eventually the team rebels. They inform management that they cannot
[L1434] continue to develop in this odious code base. They demand a redesign.
[L1435] Management does not want to expend the resources on a whole new
[L1436] redesign of the project, but they cannot deny that productivity is terrible.
[L1437] Eventually they bend to the demands of the developers and authorize the
[L1438] grand redesign in the sky.
[L1439] 
[L1440] A new tiger team is selected. Everyone wants to be on this team because it’s
[L1441] a green-field project. They get to start over and create something truly
[L1442] beautiful. But only the best and brightest are chosen for the tiger team.
[L1443] Everyone else must continue to maintain the current system.
[L1444] 
[L1445] Now the two teams are in a race. The tiger team must build a new system
[L1446] that does everything that the old system does. Not only that, they have to
[L1447] keep up with the changes that are continuously being made to the old
[L1448] system. Management will not replace the old system until the new system
[L1449] can do everything that the old system does.
[L1450] 
[L1451] This race can go on for a very long time. I’ve seen it take 10 years. And by
[L1452] the time it’s done, the original members of the tiger team are long gone, and
[L1453] the current members are demanding that the new system be redesigned
[L1454] because it’s such a mess.
[L1455] 
[L1456] If you have experienced even one small part of the story I just told, then
[L1457] you already know that spending time keeping your code clean is not just
[L1458] cost effective; it’s a matter of professional survival.
[L1459] 
[L1460] Attitude
[L1461] 
[L1462] Have you ever waded through a mess so grave that it took weeks to do what
[L1463] should have taken hours? Have you seen what should have been a one-line
[L1464] change, made instead in hundreds of different modules? These symptoms
[L1465] are all too common.
[L1466] 
[L1467] Why does this happen to code? Why does good code rot so quickly into bad
[L1468] code? We have lots of explanations for it. We complain that the
[L1469] requirements changed in ways that thwart the original design. We bemoan
[L1470] the schedules that were too tight to do things right. We blather about stupid
[L1471] managers and intolerant customers and useless marketing types and
[L1472] telephone sanitizers. But the fault, dear Dilbert, is not in our stars, but in
[L1473] ourselves. We are unprofessional.
[L1474] 
[L1475] 
[L1476] 
[L1477] This may be a bitter pill to swallow. How could this mess be our fault?
[L1478] What about the requirements? What about the schedule? What about the
[L1479] stupid managers and the useless marketing types? Don’t they bear some of
[L1480] the blame?
[L1481] 
[L1482] No. The managers and marketers look to us for the information they need to
[L1483] make promises and commitments; and even when they don’t look to us, we
[L1484] should not be shy about telling them what we think. The users look to us to
[L1485] validate the way the requirements will fit into the system. The project
[L1486] managers look to us to help work out the schedule. We are deeply complicit
[L1487] in the planning of the project and share a great deal of the responsibility for
[L1488] any failures; especially if those failures have to do with bad code!
[L1489] 
[L1490] “But wait!” you say. “If I don’t do what my manager says, I’ll be fired.”
[L1491] Probably not. Most managers want the truth, even when they don’t act like
[L1492] it. Most managers want good code, even when they are obsessing about the
[L1493] schedule. They may defend the schedule and requirements with passion; but
[L1494] that’s their job. It’s your job to defend the code with equal passion.
[L1495] 
[L1496] To drive this point home, what if you were a doctor and had a patient who
[L1497] demanded that you stop all the silly hand-washing in preparation for
[L1498] surgery because it was taking too much time?2 Clearly the patient is the
[L1499] boss; and yet the doctor should absolutely refuse to comply. Why? Because
[L1500] the doctor knows more than the patient about the risks of disease and
[L1501] infection. It would be unprofessional (never mind criminal) for the doctor to
[L1502] comply with the patient.
[L1503] 2. When hand-washing was first recommended to physicians by Ignaz Semmelweis in 1847, it was
[L1504] rejected on the basis that doctors were too busy and wouldn’t have time to wash their hands between
[L1505] patient visits.
[L1506] 
[L1507] So too it is unprofessional for programmers to bend to the will of managers
[L1508] who don’t understand the risks of making messes.

[L1510] The Primal Conundrum
[L1511] 
[L1512] Programmers face a conundrum of basic values. All developers with more
[L1513] than a few years experience know that previous messes slow them down.
[L1514] And yet all developers feel the pressure to make messes in order to meet
[L1515] deadlines. In short, they don’t take the time to go fast!
[L1516] 
[L1517] 
[L1518] 
[L1519] True professionals know that the second part of the conundrum is wrong.
[L1520] You will not make the deadline by making the mess. Indeed, the mess will
[L1521] slow you down instantly, and will force you to miss the deadline. The only
[L1522] way to make the deadline—the only way to go fast—is to keep the code as
[L1523] clean as possible at all times.
[L1524] 
[L1525] The Art of Clean Code?
[L1526] 
[L1527] Let’s say you believe that messy code is a significant impediment. Let’s say
[L1528] that you accept that the only way to go fast is to keep your code clean. Then
[L1529] you must ask yourself: “How do I write clean code?” It’s no good trying to
[L1530] write clean code if you don’t know what it means for code to be clean!
[L1531] 
[L1532] The bad news is that writing clean code is a lot like painting a picture. Most
[L1533] of us know when a picture is painted well or badly. But being able to
[L1534] recognize good art from bad does not mean that we know how to paint. So
[L1535] too being able to recognize clean code from dirty code does not mean that
[L1536] we know how to write clean code!
[L1537] 
[L1538] Writing clean code requires the disciplined use of a myriad little techniques
[L1539] applied through a painstakingly acquired sense of “cleanliness.” This
[L1540] “code-sense” is the key. Some of us are born with it. Some of us have to
[L1541] fight to acquire it. Not only does it let us see whether code is good or bad,
[L1542] but it also shows us the strategy for applying our discipline to transform bad
[L1543] code into clean code.
[L1544] 
[L1545] A programmer without “code-sense” can look at a messy module and
[L1546] recognize the mess but will have no idea what to do about it. A programmer
[L1547] with “code-sense” will look at a messy module and see options and
[L1548] variations. The “code-sense” will help that programmer choose the best
[L1549] variation and guide him or her to plot a sequence of behavior preserving
[L1550] transformations to get from here to there.
[L1551] 
[L1552] In short, a programmer who writes clean code is an artist who can take a
[L1553] blank screen through a series of transformations until it is an elegantly
[L1554] coded system.

[L14] defined interface does not offer very many functions to depend upon, so

[L19] of their classes and modules. The fewer methods a class has, the better. The

[L34] never called or switch/case conditions that never occur.

[L38] not completely updated when designs change. It still compiles, but it does
