[L32] We had a pretty good idea of where our world ended and the new world
[L33] began. As we worked, we sometimes bumped up against this boundary.
[L34] Though mists and clouds of ignorance obscured our view beyond the
[L35] boundary, our work made us aware of what we wanted the boundary
[L36] interface to be. We wanted to tell the transmitter something like this:
[L37] 
[L38] Key the transmitter on the provided frequency and emit an analog
[L39] representation of the data coming from this stream.
[L40] 
[L41] We had no idea how that would be done because the API had not been
[L42] designed yet. So we decided to work out the details later.
[L43] 
[L44] To keep from being blocked, we defined our own interface. We called it
[L45] something catchy, like Transmitter. We gave it a method called transmit that took
[L46] a frequency and a data stream. This was the interface we wished we had.
[L47] 
[L48] One good thing about writing the interface we wish we had is that it’s under
[L49] our control. This helps keep client code more readable and focused on what
[L50] it is trying to accomplish.
[L51] 
[L52] In Figure 8-2, you can see that we insulated the CommunicationsController classes
[L53] from the transmitter API (which was out of our control and undefined). By
[L54] using our own application specific interface, we kept our CommunicationsController
[L55] code clean and expressive. Once the transmitter API was defined, we wrote
[L56] the TransmitterAdapter to bridge the gap. The ADAPTER2 encapsulated the
[L57] 
[L58] 
[L59] 
[L60] interaction with the API and provides a single place to change when the
[L61] API evolves.
[L62] 2. See the Adapter pattern in [GOF].
[L63] 
[L64] Figure 8-2 Predicting the transmitter
[L65] 
[L66] This design also gives us a very convenient seam3 in the code for testing.
[L67] Using a suitable FakeTransmitter, we can test the CommunicationsController classes. We
[L68] can also create boundary tests once we have the TransmitterAPI that make sure
[L69] we are using the API correctly.
[L70] 3. See more about seams in [WELC].
[L71] 
[L72] 
[L73] 
[L74] Clean Boundaries
[L75] 
[L76] Interesting things happen at boundaries. Change is one of those things.
[L77] Good software designs accommodate change without huge investments and
[L78] rework. When we use code that is out of our control, special care must be
[L79] taken to protect our investment and make sure future change is not too
[L80] costly.

[L1] that describe significant defect reduction. From IBM, to Microsoft, from

[L4] that no professional should ignore.
[L5] Courage
[L6] 
[L7] Why don’t you fix bad code when you see it? Your first reaction upon
[L8] seeing a messy function is “This is a mess, it needs to be cleaned.” Your
[L9] second reaction is “I’m not touching it!” Why? Because you know that if
[L10] you touch it you risk breaking it; and if you break it, it becomes yours.
[L11] But what if you could be sure that your cleaning did not break anything?
[L12] What if you had the kind of certainty that I just mentioned? What if you
[L13] 
[L14] 
[L15] 
[L16] could click a button and know within 90 seconds that your changes had
[L17] broken nothing, and had only done good?
[L18] This is one of the most powerful benefits of TDD. When you have a suite of
[L19] tests that you trust, then you lose all fear of making changes. When you see
[L20] bad code, you simply clean it on the spot. The code becomes clay that you
[L21] can safely sculpt into simple and pleasing structures.
[L22] When programmers lose the fear of cleaning, they clean! And clean code is
[L23] easier to understand, easier to change, and easier to extend. Defects become
[L24] even less likely because the code gets simpler. And the code base steadily
[L25] improves instead of the normal rotting that our industry has become used to.
[L26] What professional programmer would allow the rotting to continue?
[L27] Documentation
[L28] 
[L29] Have you ever used a third-party framework? Often the third party will
[L30] send you a nicely formatted manual written by tech writers. The typical
[L31] manual employs 27 eight-by-ten color glossy photographs with circles and
[L32] arrows and a paragraph on the back of each one explaining how to
[L33] configure, deploy, manipulate, and otherwise use that framework. At the
[L34] back, in the appendix, there’s often an ugly little section that contains all the
[L35] code examples.
[L36] Where’s the first place you go in that manual? If you are a programmer, you
[L37] go to the code examples. You go to the code because you know the code
[L38] will tell you the truth. The 27 eight-by-ten color glossy photographs with
[L39] circles and arrows and a paragraph on the back might be pretty, but if you
[L40] want to know how to use code you need to read code.
[L41] Each of the unit tests you write when you follow the three laws is an
[L42] example, written in code, describing how the system should be used. If you
[L43] follow the three laws, then there will be a unit test that describes how to
[L44] create every object in the system, every way that those objects can be
[L45] created. There will be a unit test that describes how to call every function in
[L46] the system every way that those functions can meaningfully be called. For
[L47] anything you need to know how to do, there will be a unit test that describes
[L48] it in detail.
[L49] The unit tests are documents. They describe the lowest-level design of the
[L50] system. They are unambiguous, accurate, written in a language that the
[L51] audience understands, and are so formal that they execute. They are the best
[L52]

[L55] kind of low-level documentation that can exist. What professional would
[L56] not provide such documentation?

[L59] why should readers be expected to profit from them?
[L60] 
[L61] Don’t Use a Comment When You Can Use a Function or a Variable
[L62] 
[L63] Consider the following stretch of code:
[L64]    // does the module from the global list <mod> depend on the
[L65]    // subsystem we are part of?
[L66]    if (smodule.getDependSubsystems().contains(subSysMod.getSubSystem()))
[L67] 
[L68] This could be rephrased without the comment as
[L69]    ArrayList moduleDependees = smodule.getDependSubsystems();
[L70]    String ourSubSystem = subSysMod.getSubSystem();
[L71]    if (moduleDependees.contains(ourSubSystem))
[L72] 
[L73] The author of the original code may have written the comment first
[L74] (unlikely) and then written the code to fulfill the comment. However, the
[L75] author should then have refactored the code, as I did, so that the comment
[L76] could be removed.
[L77] 
[L78] Position Markers
[L79] 
[L80] Sometimes programmers like to mark a particular position in a source file.
[L81] For example, I recently found this in a program I was looking through:
[L82]    // Actions //////////////////////////////////
[L83] 
[L84] There are rare times when it makes sense to gather certain functions
[L85] together beneath a banner like this. But in general they are clutter that
[L86] should be eliminated—especially the noisy train of slashes at the end.
[L87] 
[L88] Think of it this way. A banner is startling and obvious if you don’t see
[L89] banners very often. So use them very sparingly, and only when the benefit
[L90] is significant. If you overuse banners, they’ll fall into the background noise
[L91] and be ignored.
[L92] 
[L93] Closing Brace Comments
[L94] 
[L95] Sometimes programmers will put special comments on closing braces, as in
[L96] Listing 4-6. Although this might make sense for long functions with deeply
[L97] nested structures, it serves only to clutter the kind of small and encapsulated
[L98] functions that we prefer. So if you find yourself wanting to mark your
[L99] closing braces, try to shorten your functions instead.

[L14] A cleaner way to use Map might look like the following. No user of Sensors

[L27] The interface at the boundary (Map) is hidden. It is able to evolve with very
[L28] little impact on the rest of the application. The use of generics is no longer a
[L29] big issue because the casting and type management is handled inside the
[L30] Sensors class.
[L31] 
[L32] This interface is also tailored and constrained to meet the needs of the
[L33] application. It results in code that is easier to understand and harder to
[L34] misuse. The Sensors class can enforce design and business rules.
[L35] 
[L36] We are not suggesting that every use of Map be encapsulated in this form.
[L37] Rather, we are advising you not to pass Maps (or any other interface at a
[L38] boundary) around your system. If you use a boundary interface like Map, keep
[L39] it inside the class, or close family of classes, where it is used. Avoid
[L40] returning it from, or accepting it as an argument to, public APIs.

[L44] Exploring and Learning Boundaries
[L45] 
[L46] Third-party code helps us get more functionality delivered in less time.
[L47] Where do we start when we want to utilize some third-party package? It’s
[L48] not our job to test the third-party code, but it may be in our best interest to
[L49] write tests for the third-party code we use.
[L50] 
[L51] Suppose it is not clear how to use our third-party library. We might spend a
[L52] day or two (or more) reading the documentation and deciding how we are
[L53] going to use it. Then we might write our code to use the third-party code
[L54] and see whether it does what we think. We would not be surprised to find
[L55] ourselves bogged down in long debugging sessions trying to figure out
[L56] whether the bugs we are experiencing are in our code or theirs.
[L57] 
[L58] Learning the third-party code is hard. Integrating the third-party code is
[L59] hard too. Doing both at the same time is doubly hard. What if we took a

[L62] understanding of the third-party code. Jim Newkirk calls such tests learning

[L1] The problem with dead code is that after awhile it starts to smell. The older
[L2] it is, the stronger and sourer the odor becomes. This is because dead code is
[L3] not completely updated when designs change. It still compiles, but it does
[L4] not follow newer conventions or rules. It was written at a time when the
[L5] 
[L6] 
[L7] 
[L8] system was different. When you find dead code, do the right thing. Give it a
[L9] decent burial. Delete it from the system.
[L10] 
[L11] G10: Vertical Separation
[L12] 
[L13] Variables and function should be defined close to where they are used.
[L14] Local variables should be declared just above their first usage and should
[L15] have a small vertical scope. We don’t want local variables declared
[L16] hundreds of lines distant from their usages.
[L17] 
[L18] Private functions should be defined just below their first usage. Private
[L19] functions belong to the scope of the whole class, but we’d still like to limit
[L20] the vertical distance between the invocations and definitions. Finding a
[L21] private function should just be a matter of scanning downward from the
[L22] first usage.
[L23] 
[L24] G11: Inconsistency
[L25] 
[L26] If you do something a certain way, do all similar things in the same way.
[L27] This goes back to the principle of least surprise. Be careful with the
[L28] conventions you choose, and once chosen, be careful to continue to follow
[L29] them.
[L30] 
[L31] If within a particular function you use a variable named response to hold an
[L32] HttpServletResponse, then use the same variable name consistently in the other
[L33] functions that use HttpServletResponse objects. If you name a method
[L34] processVerificationRequest, then use a similar name, such as processDeletionRequest, for the
[L35] methods that process other kinds of requests.
[L36] 
[L37] Simple consistency like this, when reliably applied, can make code much
[L38] easier to read and modify.
[L39] 
[L40] G12: Clutter
[L41] 
[L42] Of what use is a default constructor with no implementation? All it serves
[L43] to do is clutter up the code with meaningless artifacts. Variables that aren’t
[L44] used, functions that are never called, comments that add no information,
[L45] and so forth. All these things are clutter and should be removed. Keep your
[L46] source files clean, well organized, and free of clutter.
[L47] 
[L48] G13: Artificial Coupling
[L49] 
[L50] 
[L51] 
[L52] Things that don’t depend upon each other should not be artificially coupled.
[L53] For example, general enums should not be contained within more specific
[L54] classes because this forces the whole application to know about these more
[L55] specific classes. The same goes for general purpose static functions being
[L56] declared in specific classes.
[L57] 
[L58] In general an artificial coupling is a coupling between two modules that
[L59] serves no direct purpose. It is a result of putting a variable, constant, or
[L60] function in a temporarily convenient, though inappropriate, location. This is
[L61] lazy and careless.
[L62] 
[L63] Take the time to figure out where functions, constants, and variables ought
[L64] to be declared. Don’t just toss them in the most convenient place at hand
[L65] and then leave them there.
[L66] 
[L67] G14: Feature Envy
[L68] 
[L69] This is one of Martin Fowler’s code smells.6 The methods of a class should
[L70] be interested in the variables and functions of the class they belong to, and
[L71] not the variables and functions of other classes. When a method uses
[L72] accessors and mutators of some other object to manipulate the data within
[L73] that object, then it envies the scope of the class of that other object. It
[L74] wishes that it were inside that other class so that it could have direct access
[L75] to the variables it is manipulating. For example:
[L76] 6. [Refactoring].

[L1] If you work in a code base with code like this, it might not look all that bad
[L2] to you, but it is bad! When we return null, we are essentially creating work
[L3] for ourselves and foisting problems upon our callers. All it takes is one
[L4] missing null check to send an application spinning out of control.
[L5] 
[L6] Did you notice the fact that there wasn’t a null check in the second line of
[L7] that nested if statement? What would have happened at runtime if
[L8] persistentStore were null? We would have had a NullPointerException at runtime, and
[L9] either someone is catching NullPointerException at the top level or they are not.
[L10] Either way it’s bad. What exactly should you do in response to a
[L11] NullPointerException thrown from the depths of your application?
[L12] 
[L13] It’s easy to say that the problem with the code above is that it is missing a
[L14] null check, but in actuality, the problem is that it has too many. If you are
[L15] tempted to return null from a method, consider throwing an exception or
[L16] returning a SPECIAL CASE object instead. If you are calling a null-returning
[L17] method from a third-party API, consider wrapping that method with a
[L18] method that either throws an exception or returns a special case object.
[L19] 
[L20] In many cases, special case objects are an easy remedy. Imagine that you
[L21] have code like this:
[L22]    List<Employee> employees = getEmployees();
[L23]    if (employees != null) {
[L24]      for(Employee e : employees) {
[L25]        totalPay += e.getPay();
[L26]      }
[L27]    }
[L28] 
[L29] 
[L30] 
[L31] Right now, getEmployees can return null, but does it have to? If we change
[L32] getEmployee so that it returns an empty list, we can clean up the code:
[L33]    List<Employee> employees = getEmployees();
[L34]    for(Employee e : employees) {
[L35]      totalPay += e.getPay();
[L36]    }
[L37] 
[L38] Fortunately, Java has Collections.emptyList(), and it returns a predefined
[L39] immutable list that we can use for this purpose:
[L40]    public List<Employee> getEmployees() {
[L41]      if( .. there are no employees .. )
[L42]        return Collections.emptyList();
[L43]    }

parts:
In a Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) or Clean‐Onion/DDD‐style architecture, you intentionally “invert” the dependency direction so that your core (application/domain) layer knows only about abstract “ports” (interfaces), and your outer infrastructure layer provides the concrete “adapters” (implementations). Here’s the typical recipe:

---

## 1. Define Ports (Interfaces) in the Application Module

- **Location:**  
  `com.kdi.application.*` or `com.kdi.domain.*` (but _not_ under `infrastructure`)

- **Example:**  
  ```kotlin
  // application/usecase/tasks/ITaskRepository.kt
  package com.kdi.domain.repository

  import com.kdi.domain.models.entities.TaskEntity
  import com.kdi.domain.models.enums.TaskFlowStatus
  import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow

  interface ITaskRepository {
      suspend fun insertAsync(task: TaskEntity): Boolean
      suspend fun updateAsync(task: TaskEntity): Boolean
      suspend fun deleteAsync(task: TaskEntity): Boolean
      suspend fun getByIDAsync(taskGUID: String): TaskEntity?
      suspend fun getByStatusFlowAsync(status: TaskFlowStatus): Flow<List<TaskEntity>>
      suspend fun getAllFlowAsync(): Flow<List<TaskEntity>>
  }
  ```

- **Intent:**  
  Your use-cases (`TaskManager`, `CreateTaskUseCase`, etc.) depend only on this interface. They have no knowledge of databases, network, or other infrastructure.

---

## 2. Implement Adapters in the Infrastructure Module

- **Location:**  
  `com.kdi.infrastructure.*`

- **Example:**  
  ```kotlin
  // infrastructure/repository/TaskRepository.kt
  package com.kdi.infrastructure.repository

  import com.kdi.domain.models.entities.TaskEntity
  import com.kdi.domain.models.enums.TaskFlowStatus
  import com.kdi.domain.repository.ITaskRepository
  import com.kdi.infrastructure.database.middleware.ITaskDAO
  import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow
  import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map

  class TaskRepository(
      private val taskDAO: ITaskDAO
  ) : ITaskRepository {
      override suspend fun insertAsync(task: TaskEntity) = taskDAO.insert(task) > 0
      override suspend fun updateAsync(task: TaskEntity) = taskDAO.update(task) > 0
      override suspend fun deleteAsync(task: TaskEntity) = taskDAO.delete(task) > 0
      override suspend fun getByIDAsync(taskGUID: String) =
          taskDAO.findById(taskGUID)?.let { /* map to domain */ }

      override suspend fun getByStatusFlowAsync(status: TaskFlowStatus): Flow<List<TaskEntity>> =
          taskDAO.streamByStatus(status).map { /* map to domain */ }

      override suspend fun getAllFlowAsync(): Flow<List<TaskEntity>> =
          taskDAO.streamAll().map { /* map to domain */ }
  }
  ```

- **Wiring:**  
  In your DI module (e.g. Dagger `@Module` or Hilt), bind the interface to the implementation:
  ```kotlin
  @Module
  @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
  abstract class RepositoryModule {
      @Binds
      abstract fun bindTaskRepository(
          impl: TaskRepository
      ): ITaskRepository
  }
  ```

---

## 3. How It Fits Together

1. **Core Layer** (`application`/`domain`):  
   - Contains `ITaskRepository`, `CreateTaskUseCase`, `TaskManager`, domain entities, etc.  
   - No references to Room, Retrofit, SignalR, or any external I/O.

2. **Infrastructure Layer** (`infrastructure`):  
   - Implements `ITaskRepository` in `TaskRepository` (an “adapter”).  
   - Implements other ports—e.g. `ISignalRTelemetryService` in `SignalRTelemetryService`.  

3. **Dependency Inversion**:  
   - Core layer depends on abstractions (interfaces).  
   - Infrastructure layer depends on abstractions _and_ on concrete frameworks (Room, SignalR).  
   - The application’s entry point (e.g. `MainApplication`) configures DI so that whenever someone requests an `ITaskRepository`, they receive the `TaskRepository` from infrastructure.

---

### Why This Matters

- **Testability:** Your use-cases can be unit-tested by supplying in-memory or fake implementations of those Ports.  
- **Maintainability:** You can swap out adapters (e.g. switch from Room to a web API) without touching your core business logic.  
- **Separation of Concerns:** All your SQL/network/retry-logic lives in `infrastructure`; your domain remains pure.

By defining your “ports” (interfaces) in the **application/domain** packages and placing their **implementations** in the **infrastructure** packages—and wiring them only at the top level via DI—you achieve a clean, maintainable Hexagonal/DDD architecture.

This happens when multiple JARs have the same resource, in your case, the `META-INF/versions/9/OSGI-INF/MANIFEST.MF` file. To resolve it, you can adjust your `build.gradle` file. ```groovy

    pickFirst 'META-INF/versions/9/OSGI-INF/MANIFEST.MF'

thoughts.content: The user wants help with automatically aligning library versions to the proper ones for SDK 34. They’re likely using plugins and libraries through Gradle. Several options come to mind: the "dependencyUpdates" plugin could help; Gradle’s “refreshVersions” or the version catalogs (libs.versions.toml) might be useful too. I could also recommend the "com.github.ben-manes.versions" plugin or Android’s BOM (Bill of Materials), including Compose BOM or AndroidX BOM for Gradle 7+. There are various ways to do this.

To automatically align library versions for SDK 34, you can use the AndroidX BOM or Gradle Version Catalog. The "libs.versions.toml" file allows you to define BOM and aliases, and adjust versions when the compileSdk changes. Additionally, the "Gradle Dependency Updates Plugin" can help identify outdated dependencies and update them. You could also explore the "Gradle refreshVersions" plugin, which automatically uses the latest library versions. Alternatively, AndroidX BOM works well with Jetpack Compose and other AndroidX libraries.

parts:
You don’t have to manually bump each coordinate every time you target a new API level. Two complementary mechanisms can automate or centralize version alignment:

---

## 1. Use an AndroidX Bill of Materials (BOM)

Jetpack libraries publish a BOM that “pins” a consistent set of versions guaranteed to work together on a given AndroidX baseline. By declaring the BOM as a **platform** dependency, you omit explicit versions for all AndroidX artifacts:

```kotlin
dependencies {
  // Import the AndroidX BOM (replace with latest BOM version)
  implementation(platform("androidx:androidx-bom:2024.06.00"))

  // Now you can reference all AndroidX artifacts without versions:
  implementation(libs.androidx.core.ktx)          
  implementation(libs.androidx.appcompat)          
  implementation(libs.androidx.constraintlayout)   
  implementation(libs.androidx.lifecycle.livedata.ktx)
  // …etc…
}
```

The BOM will automatically pick the versions that were tested together—often including matching the latest compileSdk. Whenever you bump `compileSdk`, simply update the BOM’s version; all your AndroidX transitive versions adjust in lock-step.

---

## 2. Leverage a Version Catalog + “refreshVersions” or the Versions Plugin

If you’re already using the Gradle Version Catalog (your `libs.versions.toml`), you can couple it with a tool to keep those versions fresh:

1. **refreshVersions**  
   Add the plugin to your `settings.gradle.kts`:
   ```kotlin
   plugins {
     id("de.fayard.refreshVersions") version "0.51.0"
   }
   ```
   Then run:
   ```bash
   ./gradlew refreshVersions
   ```
   This interactively updates your `libs.versions.toml` to the latest safe versions for all dependencies you declare in `dependencies { … }`.

2. **Ben Manes Versions Plugin**  
   Include in your `build.gradle.kts`:
   ```kotlin
   plugins {
     id("com.github.ben-manes.versions") version "0.47.0"
   }
   ```
   Then:
   ```bash
   ./gradlew dependencyUpdates
   ```
   You’ll get a report of all libraries that have newer releases compatible with your constraints. You can then bulk-apply updates to your catalog.

---

### Workflow

1. **Declare** a single BOM (or version catalog) for AndroidX, Compose, or any other suite.  
2. **Automate** catalog refreshes with `refreshVersions` or run the versions report regularly in CI.  
3. **Bump** only the BOM/catalog version when you target a new `compileSdk`. All individual libraries follow automatically.

This approach minimizes manual version churn and guarantees compatibility for SDK 34 (or any future SDK) without editing every line in your `build.gradle.kts`.

parts:
The message you’re seeing:

```
Deprecated Gradle features were used in this build, making it incompatible with Gradle 9.0.
```

is **not** an Android-14 error—it’s a **Gradle deprecation warning**. Here’s what’s going on:

1. **Android 14 vs. Gradle 9**  
   - **Android 14** is the **SDK** level (API 34) you’re compiling against.  
   - **Gradle 9.0** is the **build tool** version that will ship in the future. Right now you’re on Gradle 8.14.2 (as shown in the log).

2. **What that warning means**  
   - Some of your Gradle scripts (in your `build.gradle(.kts)` files or in applied plugins) are using APIs that have been marked deprecated in Gradle 8.x.  
   - When you upgrade your project to **Gradle 9.0**, those deprecated APIs will be removed, and your build will break.

3. **How to pinpoint the deprecated usages**  
   Run your build with **all** warnings enabled:
   ```bash
   ./gradlew assembleDebug --warning-mode all
   ```
   You will see lines like:
   ```
   WARNING: The use of 'annotationProcessor' is deprecated and will be removed in Gradle 9.0; please use 'kapt' or 'ksp' instead.
   ```
   or
   ```
   WARNING: The 'lintOptions' block is deprecated and will be removed in Gradle 9.0; migrate to 'android.lint' in the new DSL.
   ```

4. **How to fix them**  
   - **Replace** any deprecated configurations with their recommended replacements.  
     - e.g. switch from `annotationProcessor("…:room-compiler")` to 
       ```kotlin
       // in Kotlin DSL
       dependencies {
         // remove:
         // annotationProcessor("androidx.room:room-compiler")
         // add:
         ksp("androidx.room:room-compiler:2.7.1")
       }
       ```
     - Migrate any old DSL blocks to the new ones (for example `lintOptions` → `android.lint`).
   - **Remove** any calls or properties that the warning output tells you are going away.

5. **When you upgrade to Gradle 9.0**  
   Once you have cleared all deprecation warnings, the “incompatible with Gradle 9.0” message will disappear, and your project will continue to build under Gradle 9 without errors.

---

**Bottom line:**  
- You can continue to compile against Android 14 (SDK 34) without issue.  
- Those “Gradle 9” errors are simply warnings that **today’s** Gradle APIs are being used in a way that will break in **tomorrow’s** Gradle 9.  
- To eliminate them, run with `--warning-mode all`, follow each warning’s fix recommendation, and re-build. Once all deprecations are addressed, you’ll be ready to move to Gradle 9 seamlessly.

In Android Studio’s settings you can disable or limit both IDE‐level and Gradle‐plugin version prompts so that you only see notifications for the channels and update types you care about:

1. **Turn off automatic IDE updates**  
   - **Windows / Linux**: **File → Settings → Appearance & Behavior → System Settings → Updates**

   - In that panel:  
     - **Update channel**: select **Stable** (so you don’t get Canary/EAP prompts).

2. **Suppress Gradle-plugin “new version” suggestions**  
   - **File → Settings → Editor → Inspections**  
   - In the tree, expand **Gradle** and **Kotlin Gradle**.  
   - Uncheck **“Gradle plugin version update”** and **“Kotlin Gradle plugin version update”** inspections.  

3. **Lock your Gradle and AGP versions in the wrapper**  
   - In your project root, run:  
     ```bash

So, the user doesn't need to update it for device installs—targetSdk and minSdk are the key factors for that.   To stop the prompts, go into Preferences > Editor > Notifications > Gradle notifications and uncheck the relevant options. Alternatively, they could simply ignore compileSdk suggestions since they don't impact actual device compatibility.

To stop the compileSdk upgrade suggestions in Android Studio, you can add `android.suppressUnsupportedCompileSdk=35` to your `gradle.properties` file. This suppresses the compatibility check and prevents the warnings. Alternatively, you could update your SDK manager to match the API level suggested (like API 35), or just remove the

parts:
Android Studio’s “Recommended action: update compileSdk to 35” banner and the Upgrade Assistant prompts are coming from the Android Gradle Plugin, not from Play-store or your device installs. They show up because AGP 8.x can opt-in to newer APIs at compile time—even though minSdk/targetSdk control actual device support. You have three simple ways to shut them off:

1. **Suppress the check in `gradle.properties`**  
   In your project’s `gradle.properties` (at the root), add:
   ```properties
   # Don’t warn or fail on compileSdk > installed API
   android.suppressUnsupportedCompileSdk=true
   ```
   This flag tells AGP to stop warning you about unsupported or “too new” compileSdk levels.

2. **Match your installed SDKs**  
   If you only have Android 14 (API 34) installed and you never plan to compile against API 35+, simply remove the Platform 35 entry from the SDK Manager. AGP will only suggest compileSdk versions that you actually have installed.  

3. **Ignore it**  
   The compileSdkVersion is purely a *compile-time* setting. It does *not* change which devices your APK can install on. As long as your `minSdk` and `targetSdk` remain correct (e.g. `minSdk 21`/`targetSdk 34`), you can safely leave `compileSdk 34` and dismiss the banner. It won’t break your app on older devices.

Choose whichever approach fits your workflow best—adding the `android.suppressUnsupportedCompileSdk` flag is typically the quickest way to stop the constant nags without losing any of your existing setup.

- And so on for each domain/DAO pair.

Yes – this pattern is very much like Entity Framework’s `DbContext.Set<TEntity>()`. In EF you do:

```csharp
DbSet<Customer> customers = context.Set<Customer>();
customers.Add(newCustomer);
var all = customers.ToList();

Here:

- **`GenericDao<E>`** plays the role of `DbSet<E>`. It exposes generic methods (`insertAsync`, `updateAsync`, `deleteAsync`, `getByIdAsync`, `getAllActiveAsync()`, etc.) for any entity type `E`.  
- **`GenericRepository<D, E>`** is analogous to writing your own wrapper over `DbContext.Set<E>()` that converts between your domain model `D` and your persistence model `E`.  
- **`DomainMapper<D, E>`** corresponds to EF’s internal mapping between your CLR classes (`Customer`) and the database schema.

So when you call:

```kotlin
val repo = GenericRepository<CustomerDto, CustomerEntity>(dao, mapper)
repo.insertAsync(customerDto)
```

– under the covers you’re doing the same generic CRUD that `DbContext.Set<CustomerEntity>()` would provide in C#.
